detail:
A review of orthostatic hypotension for cardiologists describes a field that has recently consolidated: the 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS syncope guideline and updated consensus statements reinforced one shared definition of orthostatic hypotension and a structured approach to evaluating it, including its close relative, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

On treatment, the review notes that droxidopa, a synthetic norepinephrine prodrug approved by the FDA in 2014 for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, was only the second drug ever approved for orthostatic hypotension, after midodrine in 1986. Smaller head-to-head studies have begun comparing drug options against each other and against non-drug measures, an area where larger trials are still needed.

Talk to your doctor before starting or changing any medication.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material.
summary: A cardiology review notes that recent consensus guidelines standardized how orthostatic hypotension is defined and evaluated, and that droxidopa's approval for the neurogenic form made it only the second FDA-approved drug for orthostatic hypotension.
takeaways: guidelines have standardized how oh is defined and evaluated
droxidopa joined midodrine as an approved option for neurogenic oh
studies compare drug and non-drug strategies head to head
treatment choices belong with your doctor; evidence is still developing
title: Orthostatic hypotension research: clearer definitions, targeted drugs
